Hi Avery — great to hear from you and glad the demo was useful.

Short answers up front:
- Billing: hosted embeddings are billed per vector unit (a single embedding call producing one vector), not per-token. We also surface token-equivalent metrics for mixed-use (generate + embed) reports, but line-item cost on the rate card is per-vector.
- Dimensions: base rate applies to our standard dimensions (128/256/384). Larger or custom dims (512/1024+) are supported but may land on a different rate band; they have higher storage and compute costs.
- Model eligibility: most models support multiple output dims via projection layers, but not every model is offered in every dim. We maintain a map of supported (model, dim) pairs.

I'm attaching the Q1 rate card and a short matrix mapping public models to supported dims. Ben (copied) can jump in with more technical detail on compute/quantization impacts.

Hi Avery — adding a little context from an infra perspective.

1) Per-vector vs per-token: we bill per-vector for dedicated embedding endpoints. For the hosted API, embeddings calls are priced per-response vector produced. There is an internal token cost when we run the model (prompt tokens for projection, etc.), but that is accounted for in our internal cost model and not exposed on the invoice.

2) Dimensionality: higher dims increase memory footprint and KV cache pressure during batching; they also affect storage for vector indexes (e.g., an index storing 1024-d vectors is roughly 4x the size of a 256-d vector index). On the rate card we show a standard unit for up to 384-d; 512 and 1024 are listed as "premium dims" with a per-vector uplift. For very custom sizes we can discuss a bespoke quote.

3) Model support: our curated catalog shows which open models are available in which dims; for example, Redwood-Embed-basic supports 128/256/384, but Redwood-Embed-large supports 512 and can be quantized for lower memory with a small quality tradeoff.

If you'd like, we can provide a short cost-per-100k-vectors example across dims so you can show procurement numbers.

Cheers,
Ben
